summary: Single-author paper presenting ACDC, an agent-built testing-and-repair system for Axon, a Lean-verified compiler previously generated by a coding agent (by the same author). Structure-specific tests (certificate-checker rejections, operational-semantics vs hardware differential execution, parser/printer round-trips) produce defect records that Claude Code (Opus 4.8) repair agents use to fix code and update Lean correctness proofs. Also argues, via unseen randomized testing and manual repair inspection, that neither Axon nor the repairs were reward-hacked.

claims.claim: Repair agents repaired every surfaced defect and eliminated every certificate rejection.
claims.evidence: §V-A states all surfaced defects were repaired; Tables I-IV list repairs (e.g. 5 operational-semantics/printer repairs, 13 T3a certificate repairs from 27 rejection combinations over 4,800 programs). Table footnote (line ~560): cost/time is only for the session that landed the repair, 'earlier failed/escalated attempts are excluded', so success-per-attempt is not reported.

claims.claim: Agent repairs can update machine-checked Lean proofs alongside code.
claims.evidence: Fcmp repair changed semantics/printer (+21/-5) with proofs (+24/-24); every certificate-checker repair also updated its correctness proof (§V-B, V-C). Lean proof checking provides an independent mechanical check.

claims.claim: No evidence of reward hacking in Axon or in the repairs.
claims.evidence: Inferred from (a) a small number of repairs eliminating defects on newly generated unseen random inputs and (b) the author's own inspection of each repair (§I, §V). No independent reviewer or formal criterion for 'reward hacked'.

claims.claim: Initial randomized testing shows most inputs surface defects in the agent-built compiler.
claims.evidence: §V-B: first 30-minute detect phase processed 8,200 assembly programs, 82% (6,760) triggered a defect; after 5 repairs a second phase of 4,600 programs surfaced none.
Operational-semantics phase total $19.19; parser phase $5.38, computed at published Opus 4.8 API rates; excludes failed/escalated attempts and the detect-phase compute.

patterns.note: Verified/checked compilation (Lean proofs + certificate checker) gives agents precise, mechanically checkable repair targets; agents successfully maintained proofs during repair.
Detect-repair-revalidate campaigns iterate until 30-minute (or 4-hour) clean detect windows; unmasked defects caught during repair validation.
Uses 'automated agent code audits' as one defect-surfacing technique; not evaluated separately.
Per-repair time, tokens, tool calls and dollar cost reported (successful sessions only).
Releases full repair session transcripts and ordered defect logs as an audit trail.

methodology.sample: One compiler (Axon, small language, ARM64 target); several campaigns: operational semantics/printer (8,200 + 4,600 programs), certificate checker T3a with Csmith-style generator (4,800 programs, 16 rounds), parser/printer.
methodology.baselines: None; no comparison to general-purpose repair agents without the structured defect records, or to existing compiler fuzzers' detection rates.
methodology.variance: Single campaign per target; author notes agent randomization could produce different results (§VI).
methodology.ablations: None on the information provided to repair agents (RQ2 is answered descriptively).
methodology.contamination_controls: Unseen randomized inputs used as hold-out for reward-hacking check.
methodology.languages: Lean 4 (compiler and proofs); source language is Axon's small custom language.

standards.artifacts: github.com/rinard/AxonTestAndRepair: baseline and per-campaign compiler, harness, defects, diffs, session transcripts, scripts and data (Data Availability).

biases.detail: Author built Axon (ref [17]) and ACDC with coding agents, and judges the absence of reward hacking by personal inspection; all reported numbers computed by agent-generated scripts (§V-B footnote).
Cost/time tables exclude failed or escalated repair attempts, so the 'all repaired' result hides the attempt count.
Small-language compiler built against the Livermore benchmarks; author concedes limited generalization (§VI).

coi.affiliations: National University of Singapore and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (single author).
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Claude Code / Opus 4.8 used as the agent; not the object of comparison.
coi.detail: No vendor affiliation, but the author evaluates his own previously published agent-built artifact (Axon) and concludes it was not reward-hacked, an intellectual self-interest.

verdict_reason: Strong artifact release and a mechanically checked oracle (Lean proofs) make the repair results credible for this one system, but it is a single-model, single-artifact self-study with author-judged reward-hacking analysis and survivorship in cost reporting.
applicability: Mostly does not transfer: the team is not building verified compilers, and Lean-proof maintenance is far from Java content ingestion. The transferable lesson is about harness design: repair agents work best when the oracle emits structured, localized defect records (which property failed, which component, minimal reproducer) rather than a bare test failure, and reward hacking should be checked against freshly generated, unseen inputs. For ingestion across ≥4 repos, the analogue is property-based/randomized generation of source content (malformed curricula, edge-case markup) with schema validators producing structured rejection records that agents repair against, then re-running on new random inputs before accepting a fix.
